name: Roman Republic
description: A republican system with elected magistrates, a senate of aristocrats, and popular assemblies. Power was distributed among consuls, praetors, and tribunes with annual terms.
sources: Polybius, Histories; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita

name: Roman Empire (Principate)
description: Autocratic rule disguised as restoration of the Republic. The emperor held supreme military and civil authority while maintaining senatorial institutions.
sources: Suetonius, Lives of the Caesars; Tacitus, Annals

name: Roman Social Orders
description: A rigid hierarchy of patricians, equestrians, plebeians, freedmen, and slaves. Social mobility was possible through wealth, military service, or manumission.
sources: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome

name: Roman Patria Potestas
description: The male head of household (paterfamilias) held absolute legal authority over all family members including adult sons, and controlled family property.
sources: Crook, Law and Life of Rome

name: Roman Law
description: A sophisticated legal system evolving from the Twelve Tables through juristic interpretation. Distinguished between ius civile, ius gentium, and ius naturale.
sources: Watson, The Spirit of Roman Law

name: Roman Legion System
description: Professional standing army organized into legions of approximately 5,000 men. Soldiers served 20-25 year terms and received land grants upon discharge.
sources: Goldsworthy, The Complete Roman Army

name: Roman State Religion
description: A polytheistic system with state-funded priesthoods. The pontifex maximus oversaw religious observance, and the emperor later absorbed this role.
sources: Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome

name: Roman Education
description: Education progressed from home tutoring to grammar schools (ludus) and rhetorical training. Greek tutors and pedagogues were common among the elite.
sources: Bonner, Education in Ancient Rome

name: Athenian Democracy
description: A direct democracy where male citizens participated in the Assembly (Ekklesia). Laws were proposed by the Council of 500 (Boule) chosen by lot.
sources: Hansen, The Athenian Democracy in the Age of Demosthenes

name: Athenian Social Classes
description: Athenian society divided citizens into property classes (Solonic), with metics (resident foreigners) and slaves occupying lower social positions.
sources: Ober, Mass and Elite in Democratic Athens

name: Athenian Oikos
description: The household (oikos) was the basic social unit managed by a male kyrios. Women were under guardianship of fathers, husbands, or nearest male relative.
sources: Lacey, The Family in Classical Greece

name: Athenian Law Courts
description: Popular courts (dikasteria) with large citizen juries decided cases. There was no professional judiciary; citizens prosecuted and defended cases themselves.
sources: Todd, The Shape of Athenian Law

name: Athenian Paideia
description: Boys received instruction in reading, music, and gymnastics. Higher education included rhetoric and philosophy through schools like the Academy and Lyceum.
sources: Marrou, A History of Education in Antiquity

name: Athenian State Religion
description: Civic religion centered on the polis with public festivals, sacrifices, and oracles. Priesthoods were often hereditary or filled by lot.
sources: Parker, Athenian Religion: A History

name: Spartan Dual Monarchy
description: A mixed constitution with two hereditary kings, a council of elders (Gerousia), elected ephors, and a citizen assembly (Apella). The ephors held significant executive power.
sources: Cartledge, Sparta and Lakonia

name: Spartan Social Hierarchy
description: Spartiate citizens (homoioi) were a warrior elite supported by perioikoi (free non-citizens) and helots (state-owned serfs tied to the land).
sources: Hodkinson, Property and Wealth in Classical Sparta

name: Spartan Agoge and Army
description: Males entered the agoge training system at age 7 and served in the army until 60. The phalanx formation and collective mess (syssitia) defined Spartan military life.
sources: Lazenby, The Spartan Army

name: Spartan Women's Status
description: Spartan women had more freedom than other Greek women, owning property, receiving physical training, and managing estates while men were at war or in barracks.
sources: Pomeroy, Spartan Women

name: Spartan Agoge
description: A mandatory state-run education and training program for boys from age 7 to 20. It emphasized discipline, endurance, military skills, and loyalty to Sparta.
sources: Kennell, The Gymnasium of Virtue

name: Pharaonic Government
description: A theocratic monarchy where the pharaoh was considered a living god. The vizier managed daily administration with regional nomarchs governing provinces.
sources: Kemp, Ancient Egypt: Anatomy of a Civilization

name: Ancient Egyptian Social Pyramid
description: A hierarchical society with the pharaoh at the apex, followed by priests and nobles, scribes and officials, artisans, and farmers, with slaves at the base.
sources: Wilkinson, The Rise and Fall of Ancient Egypt

name: Egyptian Priesthood
description: Temple priests served as intermediaries between gods and humans. The high priest of Amun at Thebes became so powerful as to rival the pharaoh in the New Kingdom.
key_roles: High Priest of Amun|Lector Priest|Wab Priest|God's Wife of Amun|Sem Priest
sources: Sauneron, The Priests of Ancient Egypt

name: Egyptian Family
description: Egyptian families were relatively egalitarian compared to other ancient societies. Women could own property, initiate divorce, and serve as witnesses in legal proceedings.
sources: Robins, Women in Ancient Egypt

name: Egyptian Scribal Schools
description: Education focused on training scribes through copying texts and learning hieratic and hieroglyphic writing. Literacy was rare and conferred high social status.
sources: Williams, The Archaeology of Ancient Egyptian Education

name: Egyptian Ma'at-Based Law
description: Law was based on the concept of ma'at (truth, order, justice). The vizier served as chief judge, and local councils (kenbet) resolved disputes.
sources: Allam, Egyptian Law Courts in Pharaonic and Hellenistic Times

name: Egyptian Military
description: The New Kingdom saw a professional standing army organized into divisions named after gods. Charioteers formed an elite corps, and foreign mercenaries were common.
sources: Spalinger, War in Ancient Egypt

name: Han Dynasty Imperial Government
description: A centralized bureaucratic state with the emperor at the apex. Officials were selected through recommendation and later examination, organized in a nine-rank system.
sources: Loewe, The Government of the Qin and Han Empires

name: Han Social Hierarchy
description: Society was organized into four occupational groups: scholars (shi), farmers (nong), artisans (gong), and merchants (shang), with the emperor and nobility above all.
sources: Hsu, Han Agriculture

name: Han Confucian Family
description: The patriarchal extended family was the fundamental social unit. Filial piety (xiao) was the supreme virtue, and the eldest male held authority over the household.
sources: Ebrey, The Inner Quarters

name: Han Imperial Academy
description: The Taixue (Imperial Academy) was established in 124 BCE to train officials in the Confucian classics. Local schools expanded education beyond the aristocracy.
sources: Lee, Education in Traditional China

name: Han Legal Code
description: A comprehensive legal code based on Legalist principles modified by Confucian values. Punishments ranged from fines to forced labor, mutilation, and execution.
sources: Hulswe, Remnants of Han Law

name: Han State Religion and Popular Cults
description: State religion combined ancestor worship, Confucian rituals, and cosmological beliefs. The emperor performed the Feng and Shan sacrifices as intermediary between Heaven and Earth.
sources: Loewe, Faith, Myth and Reason in Han China

name: Han Military System
description: A conscription-based military supplemented by professional soldiers and frontier garrisons. The Protector General managed relations with Central Asian peoples.
sources: de Crespigny, A Military History of Han China

name: Song Dynasty Civil Bureaucracy
description: A highly developed meritocratic bureaucracy selected through rigorous civil service examinations. The emperor governed through a council of ministers and a complex system of checks.
sources: Chaffee, The Thorny Gates of Learning in Sung China

name: Song Scholar-Gentry Society
description: The examination system created a powerful scholar-gentry class that dominated government and culture. Merchants gained wealth but lacked political prestige.
sources: Hymes, Statesmen and Gentlemen

name: Song Academy System
description: Private academies (shuyuan) supplemented state schools in preparing students for civil service exams. Neo-Confucian curriculum established by Zhu Xi became standard.
sources: Walton, Academies and Society in Southern Sung China

name: Song Merchant Guilds
description: Urban merchant guilds (hang) regulated trade, set prices, and maintained standards. They also served as mutual aid societies and represented members to the state.
sources: Shiba, Commerce and Society in Sung China

name: Song Legal Administration
description: A codified legal system building on Tang precedents, with the Xing Tong providing criminal law and the Song Hui Yao collecting administrative regulations.
sources: McKnight, Law and Order in Sung China

name: Qing Imperial Government
description: A Manchu-led dynasty governing through a dual system of Manchu and Chinese institutions. The Grand Council became the supreme policy-making body after 1729.
sources: Elliott, The Manchu Way

name: Qing Banner and Social System
description: The Eight Banners system organized Manchu, Mongol, and Chinese martial populations. Ethnic hierarchy placed Manchus above Mongols and Han Chinese.
sources: Crossley, A Translucent Mirror

name: Qing Banner Armies
description: The Eight Banners were hereditary military units that also served as administrative divisions. The Green Standard Army of Han Chinese soldiers supplemented Banner forces.
sources: Waley-Cohen, The Culture of War in China

name: Qing Gender Norms
description: Neo-Confucian ideology strictly separated inner (female) and outer (male) spheres. Foot-binding was widespread among Han women; widow chastity was highly valorized.
sources: Mann, Precious Records: Women in China's Long Eighteenth Century

name: Mongol Khanate System
description: The Great Khan held supreme authority, with the empire divided into khanates governed by Chinggisid princes. The kuriltai (assembly) legitimized succession.
sources: May, The Mongol Empire

name: Mongol Decimal Army
description: The army was organized on a decimal system: arbans (10), zuuns (100), minghans (1000), and tumens (10000). Soldiers served from age 15 to 60 with strict discipline.
sources: Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

name: Mongol Social Hierarchy
description: Society was organized around kinship and military rank. The Chinggisid lineage (altan urugh) held supreme status, followed by other noble lineages and common warriors.
sources: Allsen, Culture and Conquest in Mongol Eurasia

name: Yasa (Mongol Great Law)
description: The Yasa was a code of laws attributed to Chinggis Khan governing military discipline, commerce, religious tolerance, and social conduct across the empire.
sources: Morgan, The Mongols

name: Mongol Ger Household
description: The ger (yurt) household was the basic social unit of nomadic life. Wives managed the household and could wield significant political influence.
sources: Weatherford, The Secret History of the Mongol Queens

name: Ottoman Sultanate
description: A highly centralized imperial system with the sultan as absolute ruler. The grand vizier led the imperial council (Divan), and provincial governors (beylerbeyi) administered vast territories.
sources: Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300-1650

name: Ottoman Millet System
description: Society was organized into religious communities (millets) with internal self-governance. The askeri (military-ruling) class was distinct from the reaya (tax-paying subjects).
sources: Barkey, Empire of Difference

name: Janissary Corps
description: An elite infantry force originally composed of Christian boys taken through the devshirme system and converted to Islam. They became a powerful political force.
sources: Rhoads Murphey, Ottoman Warfare

name: Ottoman Islamic Hierarchy
description: The Sheikh ul-Islam was the supreme religious authority, issuing fatwas on the compatibility of laws with sharia. The ulema controlled education and justice.
sources: Zilfi, The Politics of Piety

name: Ottoman Kanun and Sharia
description: A dual legal system combining sultanic law (kanun) with Islamic sharia. The kanun addressed criminal, land, and tax matters not covered by religious law.
sources: Imber, Ebu's-su'ud: The Islamic Legal Tradition

name: Ottoman Medrese System
description: Medreses (Islamic colleges) trained religious scholars and state officials. The curriculum progressed from grammar and logic to theology and law.
sources: Zilfi, The Politics of Piety

name: Ottoman Guild System (Esnaf)
description: Urban guilds (esnaf) organized artisans and merchants by trade. They regulated quality, prices, and training, and participated in civic ceremonies.
sources: Faroqhi, Artisans of Empire

name: Achaemenid Imperial Administration
description: A vast empire governed through satrapies (provinces) with royal inspectors ("Eyes of the King") ensuring loyalty. Royal roads and postal system enabled central control.
sources: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander

name: Achaemenid Social Order
description: Persian society distinguished between the royal family, nobility (especially the Seven Great Families), free commoners, and dependent laborers (kurtash).
sources: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander

name: Achaemenid Imperial Army
description: A multi-ethnic army centered on the 10,000 Immortals as the elite guard. Provincial levies provided infantry, cavalry, and naval forces from across the empire.
sources: Sekunda, The Persian Army 560-330 BC

name: Achaemenid Zoroastrian Practice
description: The Magi served as priests and advisors, maintaining sacred fires and performing rituals. Zoroastrianism was the state religion though other faiths were tolerated.
sources: Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism

name: Achaemenid Royal Law
description: The king was the supreme lawgiver and judge. Local legal traditions were maintained within a framework of royal decrees (data), with royal judges appointed throughout the empire.
sources: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander

name: Inca Sapa Inca System
description: A centralized theocratic empire divided into four suyus (quarters). The Sapa Inca ruled as divine monarch, with provincial governors (tokrikoq) administering regions via a decimal hierarchy.
sources: D'Altroy, The Incas

name: Inca Ayllu-Based Hierarchy
description: Society was organized around the ayllu (kin-based community). The royal panaqas (lineages) sat at the apex, followed by provincial nobles, then commoners bound by labor obligations (mit'a).
sources: Murra, The Economic Organization of the Inka State

name: Inca State Religion
description: The Sapa Inca was considered the son of Inti (the sun). The Willaq Umu (high priest) led a hierarchy of priests managing temple estates, oracle shrines, and the calendar.
key_roles: Sapa Inca|Willaq Umu (High Priest)|Acllas (Sun Virgins)|Temple Priest|Diviner
sources: MacCormack, Religion in the Andes

name: Inca Yachayhuasi
description: The House of Learning (yachayhuasi) in Cusco trained noble youths in Quechua language, quipu accounting, history, religion, and military skills over four years.
sources: Julien, Reading Inca History

name: Inca Army
description: A massive army organized on a decimal system drawn from mit'a labor obligations. Ethnic units fought under their own leaders but were commanded by Inca generals.
sources: D'Altroy, The Incas

name: Inca Ayllu Kinship
description: The ayllu was a corporate kin group holding communal land. Marriage was typically monogamous for commoners; the Sapa Inca practiced polygyny with one primary wife (coya).
sources: Silverblatt, Moon, Sun, and Witches

name: Aztec Triple Alliance
description: The Aztec empire was a triple alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan. The tlatoani (speaker) of Tenochtitlan became paramount ruler, advised by a supreme council.
sources: Hassig, Aztec Warfare

name: Aztec Social Classes
description: Society divided into nobles (pipiltin), commoners (macehualtin), serfs (mayeque), and slaves (tlacotin). Warriors could advance through capturing enemies.
sources: Berdan, The Aztecs of Central Mexico

name: Aztec Priesthood
description: A complex priestly hierarchy maintained temples and performed elaborate rituals including human sacrifice. The two high priests of Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli held supreme religious authority.
key_roles: Quetzalcoatl Totec Tlamacazqui|Quetzalcoatl Tlaloc Tlamacazqui|Tlamacazqui (Priest)|Priestess|Fire Priest
sources: Townsend, The Aztecs

name: Aztec Warrior Orders
description: Male citizens were trained as warriors, with elite warrior orders (Eagle and Jaguar) for those who captured enemies. Military prowess determined social advancement.
sources: Hassig, Aztec Warfare

name: Aztec Calmecac and Telpochcalli
description: Two parallel school systems: calmecac for nobles (teaching priestcraft, law, writing, astronomy) and telpochcalli for commoners (teaching military skills and civic duties).
sources: Berdan, The Aztecs of Central Mexico

name: Aztec Judicial System
description: A hierarchical court system with judges appointed by the tlatoani. The cihuacoatl served as supreme judge. Laws were severe, with punishments including death for drunkenness and adultery.
sources: Offner, Law and Politics in Aztec Texcoco

name: Maya City-State System
description: The Maya were organized into independent city-states (kuchkabal) ruled by divine kings (ajaw). Each polity had its own dynasty, territory, and patron deities.
sources: Martin & Grube, Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens

name: Maya Social Stratification
description: A rigid hierarchy with the divine royal family at the top, followed by nobles (almehenob), artisans and merchants, commoners (ah chembal uinicob), and slaves (pentacob).
sources: Sharer & Traxler, The Ancient Maya

name: Maya Priestly Class
description: Priests (ah kin) maintained the calendar, performed divination, and conducted rituals. The high priest interpreted astronomical events and advised the king on auspicious dates.
sources: Coe, The Maya

name: Maya Elite Education
description: Noble children were educated in scribal arts, astronomy, mathematics (including the concept of zero), and ritual knowledge. Scribes (ah tz'ib) held high status.
sources: Coe & Van Stone, Reading the Maya Glyphs

name: Maya Lineage Groups
description: Elite families traced descent patrilineally through named lineages. Marriage alliances between city-states cemented political relationships, and queens could serve as regents.
sources: Schele & Freidel, A Forest of Kings

name: Maurya Imperial Administration
description: Chandragupta Maurya created a centralized bureaucratic state described in Kautilya's Arthashastra. The empire was divided into provinces, districts, and villages with appointed officials.
sources: Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas

name: Maurya Varna and Jati System
description: The four varnas (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) provided ideological framework, while jatis (birth groups) determined actual social position and occupation.
sources: Thapar, Early India

name: Maurya-Era Religious Pluralism
description: Brahmins, Buddhist monks, and Jain ascetics competed for royal patronage. Ashoka's edicts promoted dharma (moral law) and religious tolerance across the empire.
sources: Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas

name: Arthashastra Legal Framework
description: The Arthashastra outlined a comprehensive legal code covering criminal law, civil disputes, commercial regulations, and espionage. The king was the supreme judicial authority.
sources: Kautilya, Arthashastra (trans. Rangarajan)

name: Maurya Imperial Army
description: One of the largest ancient armies, organized into infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephant corps. A war office of thirty members oversaw military operations.
sources: Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas

name: Mughal Imperial System
description: A centralized autocracy with the emperor holding absolute power. The mansabdari system assigned military and revenue ranks to officials, creating a merit-based but hierarchical bureaucracy.
sources: Richards, The Mughal Empire

name: Mughal Mansabdari System
description: Officials were ranked by mansab (numerical rank) determining their salary, military obligations, and status. The system allowed social mobility for talented administrators and warriors.
sources: Athar Ali, The Mughal Nobility Under Aurangzeb

name: Mughal Religious Administration
description: Islamic scholars and Sufi saints held great influence. Akbar created the Din-i-Ilahi syncretic faith, while Aurangzeb emphasized orthodox Sunni Islam.
sources: Eaton, India in the Persianate Age

name: Mughal Military
description: A large composite army combining Mughal cavalry, Rajput warriors, artillery corps, and war elephants. The mansabdari system linked military command to administrative rank.
sources: Gommans, Mughal Warfare

name: Mughal Maktab and Madrasa
description: Education combined Islamic learning with Persian literary culture. The madrasa system taught theology, law, logic, and science, while maktabs provided basic literacy.
sources: Alam, The Languages of Political Islam in India

name: English Feudal Monarchy
description: The king ruled through a feudal hierarchy of lords, backed by the Curia Regis. Parliament gradually emerged as a legislative body with the House of Lords and Commons.
sources: Holt, Magna Carta

name: English Feudal Hierarchy
description: A pyramidal structure: king, tenants-in-chief, mesne lords, knights, free tenants, villeins (serfs), and cottars. Land tenure defined social relationships.
sources: Bloch, Feudal Society

name: English Common Law
description: The common law developed through royal courts, circuit judges, and legal precedent. Magna Carta (1215) established principles of due process and limits on royal power.
sources: Baker, An Introduction to English Legal History

name: English Medieval Church
description: The Church of England was part of the Roman Catholic hierarchy. Bishops held both spiritual and temporal power, sitting in the House of Lords.
sources: Moorman, A History of the Church in England

name: English Feudal Levy and Longbow Army
description: Military service was a feudal obligation. The development of the longbow and professional retinues transformed English warfare, especially during the Hundred Years' War.
sources: Prestwich, Armies and Warfare in the Middle Ages

name: English Medieval Household
description: The manor household was the basic economic and social unit. Primogeniture determined inheritance; younger sons entered the church, military, or sought their own fortunes.
sources: Given-Wilson, The English Nobility in the Late Middle Ages

name: English Craft Guilds
description: Urban craft guilds regulated trade, trained apprentices, and maintained quality standards. They held monopolies, participated in civic governance, and organized mystery plays.
sources: Epstein, Wage Labor and Guilds in Medieval Europe

name: French Capetian Monarchy
description: The French kings gradually centralized power from feudal lords, establishing royal courts (parlement), a professional bureaucracy, and tax collection under baillis and seneschals.
sources: Hallam, Capetian France

name: Three Estates of France
description: French society was divided into three estates: the First Estate (clergy), Second Estate (nobility), and Third Estate (commoners, including bourgeoisie and peasants).
sources: Duby, The Three Orders: Feudal Society Imagined

name: French Noble Lineage
description: Aristocratic families emphasized patrilineal descent and heraldic identity. Younger sons often entered the Church or sought marriage alliances to maintain family honor.
sources: Bouchard, Strong of Body, Brave and Noble

name: French Parlements
description: Royal parlements served as courts of appeal and registered royal edicts. The Parlement of Paris was the most powerful, with authority to block legislation.
sources: Shennan, The Parlement of Paris

name: Holy Roman Empire
description: A decentralized polity where the emperor was elected by seven prince-electors. Imperial authority was balanced against territorial princes, free cities, and the Imperial Diet.
sources: Wilson, Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire

name: Imperial Estates Hierarchy
description: The Reichstag organized estates into electors, ecclesiastical princes, secular princes, counts, prelates, and free imperial cities, each with defined rights and privileges.
sources: Stollberg-Rilinger, The Holy Roman Empire

name: Imperial Court System
description: The Reichskammergericht (Imperial Chamber Court) and Reichshofrat (Aulic Council) provided imperial justice. Roman law was received and blended with Germanic custom.
sources: Whaley, Germany and the Holy Roman Empire

name: HRE Post-Reformation Settlement
description: After 1555 (Peace of Augsburg) and 1648 (Peace of Westphalia), the principle of cuius regio eius religio allowed princes to determine their territory's religion.
sources: Schilling, Religion, Political Culture and the Emergence of Early Modern Society

name: Norse Thing Assembly
description: Viking-Age Scandinavia governed through assemblies (things) at local, regional, and national levels. Free men could speak and vote; the Althing of Iceland was a national assembly.
sources: Byock, Viking Age Iceland

name: Norse Social Classes
description: Society divided into jarls (earls/nobility), karls (free farmers and warriors), and thralls (slaves). Social mobility was possible through trade, warfare, and royal service.
sources: Brink & Price, The Viking World

name: Norse Warband (Hird)
description: The hird was a retinue of warriors sworn to a chieftain or king. Viking warfare relied on raiding parties, longship crews, and the shield wall formation.
sources: Price, The Viking Way

name: Norse Kinship and Household
description: Extended family groups (aett) shared collective responsibility including blood feud obligations. Farms were the basic economic unit, and women had significant property rights.
sources: Jochens, Women in Old Norse Society

name: Norse Law Codes
description: Oral laws were memorized by lawspeakers and later codified (e.g., Gragas in Iceland). Disputes were settled at the thing through arbitration, compensation, or outlawry.
sources: Dennis, Foote & Perkins, Laws of Early Iceland

name: Norse Pagan Practice
description: Norse religion had no centralized priesthood. Chieftains (godar) performed sacrifices (blot) at seasonal festivals, and seeresses (volur) practiced divination.
sources: Price, The Viking Way

name: Tokugawa Shogunate
description: The shogun ruled Japan through a military government (bakufu) while the emperor remained a figurehead in Kyoto. The sankin-kotai system required daimyo to maintain residences in Edo.
sources: Totman, Early Modern Japan

name: Edo Period Four-Class System
description: The rigid shi-no-ko-sho hierarchy placed samurai (shi) above farmers (no), artisans (ko), and merchants (sho). Outcaste groups (eta/hinin) existed below this system.
sources: Vaporis, Tour of Duty: Samurai, Military Service in Edo and the Culture of Early Modern Japan

name: Edo Ie (Household) System
description: The ie (household) was the fundamental social unit, headed by a male patriarch. Succession followed primogeniture; adoption was common to ensure household continuity.
sources: Nakane, Kinship and Economic Organization in Rural Japan

name: Edo Period Education
description: Han schools (hanko) educated samurai in Confucian classics and martial arts. Temple schools (terakoya) provided basic literacy to commoners, achieving high literacy rates.
sources: Dore, Education in Tokugawa Japan

name: Edo Merchant Houses and Za
description: Merchant families operated through hereditary houses (ie) governed by house codes (kakun). Professional guilds (za) regulated trade, and monopoly associations (kabu nakama) controlled markets.
sources: Crawcour, The Development of a Credit System in 17th Century Japan

name: Meiji Constitutional Monarchy
description: The Meiji Restoration created a constitutional monarchy with an elected Diet, appointed Privy Council, and powerful genro (elder statesmen) advising the emperor.
sources: Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan

name: Meiji Modern Army
description: Conscription replaced the samurai monopoly on arms. The army was modeled on the Prussian system, with a general staff, modern weapons, and national military service.
key_roles: Emperor|Chief of General Staff|General|Division Commander|Conscript Soldier
sources: Lone, Army, Empire and Politics in Meiji Japan

name: Meiji Education System
description: The 1872 Fundamental Code of Education established universal compulsory schooling. Imperial universities trained elites, while normal schools produced teachers for a national system.
key_roles: Education Minister|Imperial University President|Normal School Director|Elementary Teacher|Student
sources: Marshall, Learning to be Modern

name: Joseon Confucian Monarchy
description: A Neo-Confucian monarchy with the king ruling through the State Council (Uijeongbu) and Six Ministries. The Censorate monitored government conduct and could criticize the king.
sources: Palais, Confucian Statecraft and Korean Institutions

name: Joseon Yangban System
description: A rigid four-tier system: yangban (scholar-officials), chungin (technical specialists), sangmin (commoners), and cheonmin (lowborn). Yangban status required passing civil examinations.
sources: Deuchler, The Confucian Transformation of Korea

name: Joseon Confucian Family
description: Strict patrilineal descent with elaborate ancestor veneration. Eldest sons inherited primary responsibility; women's status declined from early to late Joseon under Neo-Confucian norms.
sources: Deuchler, The Confucian Transformation of Korea

name: Joseon Seowon Academy System
description: Private academies (seowon) and state schools (hyanggyo) prepared yangban for civil service examinations (gwageo) based on the Confucian Four Books and Five Classics.
key_roles: Academy Master|State School Teacher|Gwageo Examiner|Yangban Student
sources: Haboush, The Memoirs of Lady Hyegyong

name: Joseon Legal Code (Gyeongguk Daejeon)
description: The Grand Code for State Administration codified criminal and administrative law. Confucian principles of moral suasion were preferred over harsh punishment.
sources: Palais, Confucian Statecraft and Korean Institutions

name: Khmer Devaraja System
description: The Khmer Empire was ruled by a god-king (devaraja) whose legitimacy derived from Hindu-Buddhist cosmology. A complex bureaucracy managed irrigation, temples, and provinces.
sources: Coe, Angkor and the Khmer Civilization

name: Khmer Social Hierarchy
description: Inscriptions reveal a layered society of royalty, Brahmin priests, officials, free farmers, and temple slaves (khnhom). Temple foundations supported thousands of workers.
sources: Vickery, Society, Economics and Politics in Pre-Angkor Cambodia

name: Khmer Hindu-Buddhist Synthesis
description: A syncretic religious system combining Shaivite Hinduism and Mahayana/Theravada Buddhism. Royal temple-mountains served as cosmic centers linking king, gods, and cosmos.
sources: Harris, Cambodian Buddhism: History and Practice

name: Khmer Imperial Army
description: A large army including war elephants, cavalry, and infantry drawn from subject populations. Naval forces operated on the Tonle Sap and coastal waters.
sources: Coe, Angkor and the Khmer Civilization

name: Khmer Bilateral Kinship
description: Unlike many Southeast Asian neighbors, Khmer society practiced bilateral kinship. Women held property rights, and matrilineal elements persisted alongside patrilineal royal succession.
sources: Jacobsen, Lost Goddesses: The Denial of Female Power in Cambodian History

name: Mali Empire Administration
description: Founded by Sundiata Keita, the Mali Empire was governed by a mansa (king) with a council of clan elders. The empire was divided into provinces under appointed governors.
sources: Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali

name: Mande Social Caste System
description: Mande society was organized into horon (freeborn), nyamakala (endogamous artisan castes including griots, smiths, and leatherworkers), and jon (slaves).
sources: Conrad, Empires of Medieval West Africa

name: Mali Islamic Practice
description: Islam coexisted with traditional Mande religion. The mansa patronized Islamic scholars while maintaining traditional ritual roles, as seen in Mansa Musa's famous pilgrimage.
sources: Gomez, African Dominion

name: Sankore University and Islamic Learning
description: Timbuktu became a major center of Islamic scholarship under Mali and later Songhai. The University of Sankore attracted scholars from across the Islamic world.
sources: Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire

name: Mande Nyamakala Artisan Castes
description: Endogamous artisan castes (nyamakala) held specialized knowledge. Griots preserved oral history and genealogy; smiths were feared for their control of transformative fire.
sources: McNaughton, The Mande Blacksmiths

name: Mande Extended Family
description: The lu (household compound) organized around a patrilineal extended family under an elder. The clan (jamu) linked dispersed family groups sharing a common surname and origin story.
sources: Bird & Kendall, The Mande Hero

name: Great Zimbabwe State
description: A Shona-speaking state centered on the Great Zimbabwe stone complex. The mambo (king) controlled gold trade, cattle wealth, and religious authority over the surrounding territory.
sources: Pikirayi, The Zimbabwe Culture

name: Great Zimbabwe Social Order
description: An elite class controlled the stone-walled enclosures and long-distance trade, while commoners lived in surrounding settlements. Cattle ownership indicated wealth and status.
sources: Huffman, Snakes and Crocodiles: Power and Symbolism in Ancient Zimbabwe

name: Shona Spirit Mediums
description: The Mwari (creator god) cult and ancestor spirit mediums (svikiro) legitimized political power. Spirit mediums communicated with tribal ancestors on behalf of the community.
sources: Ranger, Voices from the Rocks

name: Shona Patrilineal Household
description: The homestead (musha) was organized around a patrilineal extended family. Bride wealth (roora) in cattle formalized marriages and created alliances between lineages.
sources: Bourdillon, The Shona Peoples

name: Zulu Kingdom
description: Shaka kaSenzangakhona created a centralized military kingdom, replacing clan-based governance with royal authority over age-regiments (amabutho) and appointed district chiefs.
sources: Hamilton, The Mfecane Aftermath

name: Zulu Impi System
description: Age-based regiments (amabutho) organized all males into military units that served the king. The bull-horn formation (impondo zankomo) was a devastating tactical innovation.
sources: Knight, The Anatomy of the Zulu Army

name: Zulu Social Organization
description: Society centered on the king and royal household, with clan chiefs subordinated to royal authority. Age regiments cut across clan lines, binding young men to the king.
sources: Guy, The Destruction of the Zulu Kingdom

name: Zulu Age-Regiment System
description: Males were organized into age-regiments (amabutho) at adolescence, living in royal barracks until the king granted permission to marry, usually around age 35-40.
sources: Morris, The Washing of the Spears

name: Zulu Umuzi Homestead
description: The umuzi (homestead) was headed by a male patriarch who could have multiple wives. Cattle were central to social transactions including lobola (bride price).
sources: Krige, The Social System of the Zulus

name: Igbo Village Democracy
description: Most Igbo communities lacked centralized authority, governing through village assemblies, councils of elders, titled societies, and age grades in a diffuse political system.
key_roles: Obi (Village Head)|Council of Elders|Age Grade Leader|Title Holder (Ozo)|Dibia (Priest)
sources: Uchendu, The Igbo of Southeast Nigeria

name: Igbo Achievement-Based Status
description: Status was earned rather than inherited. Men gained prestige through title-taking (ozo), wealth accumulation, and community service. No hereditary aristocracy existed.
sources: Isichei, A History of the Igbo People

name: Igbo Age Grade System
description: Age grades organized males into groups that progressed through defined social roles from youth labor to warrior service to elder council membership over a lifetime.
key_roles: Senior Elder Grade|Warrior Grade|Young Adult Grade|Youth Grade
sources: Uchendu, The Igbo of Southeast Nigeria

name: Igbo Compound Family
description: The compound (obi) housed a patrilineal extended family. Women moved to their husband's compound at marriage but maintained ties to their natal family.
sources: Amadiume, Male Daughters, Female Husbands

name: Igbo Dual-Sex Political System
description: Women had their own parallel political organizations. The Umu Ada (daughters of the lineage) and Otu Alutaradi (wives' associations) held real authority in women's affairs.
key_roles: Umu Ada Leader|Senior Wife|Market Women Leader|Age Grade Woman|Dibia (Priestess)
sources: Amadiume, Male Daughters, Female Husbands

name: Igbo Traditional Religion
description: A decentralized religious system with Chukwu as supreme deity, Ala (earth goddess) as moral enforcer, and local deities (alusi) served by priests and oracles.
key_roles: Eze Nri (Ritual Leader)|Dibia (Priest-Diviner)|Oracle Priest|Masquerade Society Leader
sources: Isichei, A History of the Igbo People

name: Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace
description: The Iroquois Confederacy united five (later six) nations under the Gayanashagowa (Great Law of Peace). Fifty hereditary sachems governed by consensus at grand councils.
key_roles: Hoyane (Sachem)|Clan Mother|War Chief|Pine Tree Chief|Faith Keeper
sources: Fenton, The Great Law and the Longhouse

name: Haudenosaunee Clan Mother Authority
description: Clan Mothers held enormous power: they nominated and could depose sachems, controlled longhouse resources, decided the fate of captives, and approved declarations of war.
sources: Mann, Iroquoian Women: The Gantowisas

name: Haudenosaunee Longhouse Family
description: Matrilocal extended families lived in longhouses organized by clan. Clan mothers managed domestic affairs and food distribution while men hunted and engaged in diplomacy.
sources: Snow, The Iroquois

name: Haudenosaunee Condolence and Restitution
description: Justice focused on restitution rather than punishment. The condolence ceremony healed grief from wrongdoing, and the Clan Mother's council mediated disputes between families.
sources: Richter, The Ordeal of the Longhouse

name: Haudenosaunee Longhouse Religion
description: The Longhouse Religion (Gaihwi:io) combined traditional ceremonial cycles with Handsome Lake's Code. Faith Keepers maintained the ceremonial calendar and conducted seasonal rites.
sources: Wallace, The Death and Rebirth of the Seneca

name: Haudenosaunee War Party
description: War chiefs were chosen for their skill and following, distinct from peacetime sachems. War parties were voluntary; warriors could withdraw at any point before engagement.
key_roles: War Chief|Pine Tree Chief|Warrior|Scout|Clan Mother (War Approval)
sources: Richter, The Ordeal of the Longhouse

name: Hawaiian Chiefdom
description: A stratified Polynesian chiefdom where the ali'i nui (paramount chief) ruled through divine authority (mana). The kapu (taboo) system regulated social interactions and resource management.
key_roles: Ali'i Nui (Paramount Chief)|Ali'i (Chief)|Kahuna Nui (High Priest)|Konohiki (Land Manager)|Maka'ainana (Commoner)
sources: Kirch, How Chiefs Became Kings

name: Hawaiian Caste System
description: A rigid hierarchy: ali'i (chiefly class), kahuna (priestly/expert class), maka'ainana (commoners), and kauwa (outcaste/slaves). Rank was determined by genealogical proximity to the gods.
sources: Sahlins, Historical Metaphors and Mythical Realities

name: Hawaiian Kapu System
description: The kapu system enforced sacred prohibitions linked to divine authority. The kahuna nui (high priest) managed temple (heiau) rituals, including the Makahiki festival honoring Lono.
key_roles: Ali'i Nui|Kahuna Nui|Kahuna Pule (Prayer Priest)|Kahuna Kalai (Temple Builder)
sources: Valeri, Kingship and Sacrifice

name: Hawaiian Ohana
description: The ohana (extended family) was the basic social unit, often including adopted members. Chiefs practiced sacred sibling marriage (pi'o) to concentrate divine mana.
key_roles: Ali'i (Chief Parent)|Haku (Household Head)|Keiki Hanai (Adopted Child)|Ohana Member
sources: Handy & Pukui, The Polynesian Family System in Ka-'u

name: Hawaiian Gender and Kapu
description: The aikapu (eating kapu) separated men and women during meals and prohibited women from eating certain foods (pork, bananas, coconut). Kamehameha II abolished this in 1819.
sources: Linnekin, Sacred Queens and Women of Consequence

name: Maori Tribal Authority
description: Maori society was organized into iwi (tribes), hapu (sub-tribes), and whanau (families). Rangatira (chiefs) led through mana (prestige) and consensus rather than coercion.
sources: Walker, Ka Whawhai Tonu Matou: Struggle Without End

name: Maori Social Ranks
description: Three broad ranks: rangatira (chiefly families), tutua/ware (commoners), and taurekareka (captives/slaves). Mana was inherited but also earned through achievement.
sources: Ballara, Iwi: The Dynamics of Maori Tribal Organisation

name: Maori Whanau
description: The whanau (extended family) was the primary social and economic unit. Both patrilineal and matrilineal descent were recognized, with individuals choosing which lineage to emphasize.
sources: Metge, New Growth from Old

name: Maori Taua (War Party)
description: War parties were organized by hapu under war leaders (toa). Pa (fortified villages) were sophisticated defensive works. Warfare was linked to utu (reciprocity) and mana.
sources: Vayda, Maori Warfare

name: Maori Tohunga and Tapu
description: Tohunga (experts/priests) maintained sacred knowledge, performed rituals, and managed tapu (sacred restrictions). Different tohunga specialized in healing, navigation, or warfare.
sources: Best, The Maori

name: Aboriginal Australian Elders Council
description: Aboriginal governance was based on councils of initiated elders who held sacred knowledge. Authority derived from ceremonial status, not coercive power, with decisions made by consensus.
sources: Berndt & Berndt, The World of the First Australians

name: Aboriginal Section/Subsection System
description: Complex marriage class systems (moiety, section, or subsection) regulated kinship, marriage, and ceremonial obligations across the entire social landscape.
sources: Tonkinson, The Mardu Aborigines

name: Aboriginal Initiation Grades
description: Males progressed through initiation stages gaining sacred knowledge and ceremonial authority. Full initiation could take decades, with each stage unlocking new rights and responsibilities.
key_roles: Fully Initiated Elder|Senior Initiate|Junior Initiate|Uninitiated Youth
sources: Elkin, The Australian Aborigines

name: Aboriginal Dreamtime Custodianship
description: Knowledge of Dreamtime stories and associated sacred sites was held by custodians who maintained the cosmic order through ceremony, song, and ritual performance.
key_roles: Senior Custodian|Song Line Keeper|Clever Man (Maban)|Ceremonial Leader|Initiated Man
sources: Strehlow, Songs of Central Australia

name: Aboriginal Gender Complementarity
description: Men's and women's ceremonial lives were largely separate but complementary. Women held their own sacred knowledge, ceremonies, and authority over women's business.
key_roles: Senior Initiated Man|Senior Woman|Male Ceremonial Leader|Female Ceremonial Leader
sources: Bell, Daughters of the Dreaming

name: Aboriginal Customary Law
description: Dispute resolution relied on mediation by elders, ritualized combat, and sorcery accusations. Serious breaches of law were punished through spearing or ostracism.
sources: Berndt & Berndt, The World of the First Australians

name: Nuer Segmentary Lineage System
description: The Nuer had no centralized authority, organizing through nested segments of lineages that united or opposed each other depending on the level of conflict. Leopard-skin chiefs mediated disputes.
sources: Evans-Pritchard, The Nuer

name: Nuer Cattle-Based Kinship
description: Cattle were central to all social transactions: bride wealth, blood compensation, and sacrifice. Ghost marriage and woman-to-woman marriage expanded kinship possibilities.
sources: Evans-Pritchard, Kinship and Marriage Among the Nuer

name: Nuer Age-Set System
description: Males were initiated into named age-sets through scarification ceremonies. Age-sets progressed through warrior, elder, and senior elder stages with defined social roles.
sources: Evans-Pritchard, The Nuer

name: Nuer Prophets and Spirits
description: Prophets (guk) claimed possession by spirits of the Above (kwoth nhial) and gained political influence during crises. Earth priests maintained local shrines.
sources: Johnson, Nuer Prophets

name: Nuer Gender and Cattle
description: Men controlled cattle and political life while women managed the domestic sphere and agriculture. However, woman-to-woman marriage allowed women to become social fathers.
sources: Evans-Pritchard, Kinship and Marriage Among the Nuer

name: Maasai Age-Set Governance
description: The Maasai had no centralized political authority. Governance operated through age-sets, elder councils, and ritual specialists (laibon) who provided guidance and prophecy.
sources: Spear & Waller, Being Maasai

name: Maasai Age-Set System
description: Males progressed through defined age-grades: boys (ilayiok), junior warriors (ilmurran), senior warriors, junior elders, and senior elders. Each transition involved elaborate ceremonies.
sources: Spencer, The Maasai of Matapato

name: Maasai Moran Warrior System
description: Young men spent 10-15 years as moran (warriors), living in manyattas (warrior camps) separate from their families. They defended territory, raided cattle, and hunted lions.
key_roles: Senior Moran Leader|Moran|Junior Moran|Moran Camp Leader
sources: Spencer, The Maasai of Matapato

name: Maasai Enkang Homestead
description: The enkang (homestead) was a circular thorn-fenced compound containing houses of a man's wives. Women built and owned houses; men controlled cattle.
sources: Hodgson, Once Intrepid Warriors

name: Maasai Oloiboni and Enkai
description: The Maasai worshipped Enkai (God), with the oloiboni (ritual specialist/diviner) serving as intermediary. The oloiboni lineage of Supeet held hereditary spiritual authority.
sources: Berntsen, The Maasai and Their Neighbors

name: Maasai Gender Organization
description: Maasai society assigned complementary roles: men herded cattle and made political decisions; women built houses, milked cows, raised children, and managed domestic resources.
sources: Hodgson, Once Intrepid Warriors

name: !Kung San Band Organization
description: Small, flexible bands of 25-50 people with no formal leaders. Decisions were made through discussion and consensus. Informal leaders emerged based on hunting skill and persuasive ability.
sources: Lee, The !Kung San

name: !Kung San Bilateral Kinship
description: Bilateral kinship with flexible residence patterns. Couples could live with either spouse's family. Name-sharing (namesakes) created fictive kinship bonds across bands.
sources: Lee, The Dobe Ju/'hoansi

name: !Kung San Egalitarian Gender
description: Relatively egalitarian gender relations. Women's gathering provided 60-80% of calories. Both sexes participated in decision-making, though men monopolized hunting.
sources: Shostak, Nisa: The Life and Words of a !Kung Woman

name: !Kung San Trance Healing
description: Healing dances involved trance states (kia) where healers accessed n/om (spiritual energy). Approximately half of men and a third of women became healers.
sources: Katz, Boiling Energy

name: !Kung San Conflict Resolution
description: Disputes were resolved through prolonged discussion, mediation by respected individuals, and social pressure. Persistent offenders faced ostracism or, in extreme cases, execution by group consensus.
sources: Lee, The !Kung San

name: Trobriand Chieftainship
description: Chiefs of the Tabalu clan held highest rank in a system where rank derived from matrilineal clan membership. Chiefs accumulated wealth through polygynous marriages and yam exchanges.
sources: Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific

name: Trobriand Matrilineal Kinship
description: Descent was traced through the mother's line (dala). A child's social identity came from the mother's clan, while the father's role was nurturing rather than biological in Trobriand ideology.
sources: Weiner, Women of Value, Men of Renown

name: Trobriand Women's Wealth
description: Women controlled their own form of wealth (banana-leaf bundles and skirts) distributed at mortuary ceremonies. This women's wealth was essential for cosmic reproduction of the clan.
sources: Weiner, Women of Value, Men of Renown

name: Trobriand Kula Exchange
description: The Kula ring was an inter-island exchange system of shell valuables (necklaces and armbands). Participation conferred prestige and established trading partnerships across hundreds of miles.
sources: Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific

name: Trobriand Magic and Sorcery
description: Garden magic ensured agricultural success, while sorcery (bwagau) was feared as a cause of death. Knowledge of spells was inherited matrilineally and closely guarded.
key_roles: Chief Sorcerer (Bwagau)|Garden Magician|Canoe Magician|Weather Magician|Love Magician
sources: Malinowski, Coral Gardens and Their Magic

name: Byzantine Imperial Administration
description: A continuation of Roman imperial government with Christian theocratic elements. The emperor was God's representative on earth, supported by a complex bureaucracy of logothetes and strategoi.
sources: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society

name: Byzantine Social Order
description: A hierarchy of emperor, senatorial aristocracy, urban professionals, peasant farmers, and slaves. The dynatoi (powerful) landowners increasingly dominated the provinces.
sources: Kazhdan & Wharton Epstein, Change in Byzantine Culture

name: Byzantine Orthodox Church
description: The Patriarch of Constantinople led the church with the emperor's support. The Ecumenical Councils defined dogma, and monasticism was a powerful spiritual and economic force.
sources: Meyendorff, Byzantine Theology

name: Byzantine Theme System
description: After the 7th century, the empire was reorganized into themes (military-administrative provinces). Each theme was commanded by a strategos who combined military and civil authority.
sources: Haldon, Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World

name: Byzantine Roman Law (Corpus Juris Civilis)
description: Justinian's codification of Roman law remained the basis of Byzantine jurisprudence. Later compilations like the Ecloga and Basilika adapted the law to changing conditions.
sources: Humfress, Orthodoxy and the Courts in Late Antiquity

name: Byzantine Imperial University
description: The University of Constantinople trained bureaucrats and scholars in classical Greek literature, philosophy, rhetoric, and law. The church also maintained theological schools.
sources: Markopoulos, Education in Byzantium

name: Abbasid Caliphate Administration
description: The caliph ruled as both political and religious leader, though real power often lay with the vizier and later with military commanders (emirs). A sophisticated bureaucracy managed the empire.
sources: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates

name: Abbasid Social Hierarchy
description: Arab Muslims initially held the highest status, but Persian, Turkish, and other converts achieved high positions. Dhimmis (protected peoples), slaves, and freedmen occupied lower rungs.
sources: Lapidus, A History of Islamic Societies

name: Abbasid Islamic Scholarly Hierarchy
description: The ulama (religious scholars) developed the major schools of Islamic jurisprudence (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali). Sufi orders emerged as popular mystical movements.
sources: Berkey, The Formation of Islam

name: Abbasid House of Wisdom and Madrasa
description: The Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts. Madrasas formalized Islamic education in theology, law, and the sciences.
sources: Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture

name: Abbasid Sharia Courts
description: Islamic law was administered through qadi courts applying the major madhab (legal schools). The muhtasib enforced public morality and market regulations.
sources: Hallaq, The Origins and Evolution of Islamic Law

name: Abbasid Artisan Guilds
description: Urban guilds (sinf/hirfa) organized craftsmen and merchants by trade. They regulated quality, set prices, and were overseen by the muhtasib (market inspector).
sources: Floor, The Guilds and Futuwwa in Iran

name: Abbasid Mamluk and Ghulam System
description: The Abbasids increasingly relied on slave soldiers (mamluks/ghulams), particularly Turks, who rose to become generals and de facto rulers, undermining caliphal authority.
key_roles: Caliph|Commander of the Faithful's Guard|Turkish General|Mamluk Commander|Ghulam|Foot Soldier
sources: Gordon, The Breaking of a Thousand Swords

name: Songhai Imperial Administration
description: The Askia dynasty ruled through a centralized bureaucracy with provincial governors, tax collectors, and a system of Islamic judges. The askia served as both political and religious leader.
sources: Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire

name: Songhai Social Stratification
description: Society was divided into free nobles, scholars, merchants, artisan castes, and dependent populations (slaves and captives). Islamic scholars held high prestige.
sources: Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali

name: Songhai Islamic Authority
description: Islam was the state religion. Timbuktu and Djenne were centers of Islamic learning, with powerful qadis and ulama exercising judicial and moral authority.
key_roles: Askia|Chief Qadi of Timbuktu|Imam|Ulama Scholar|Sufi Sheikh
sources: Gomez, African Dominion

name: Songhai Islamic Scholarship
description: Timbuktu's mosques and madrasas attracted scholars from across the Sahel and North Africa. Ahmad Baba was among the most renowned scholars of the late Songhai period.
sources: Saad, Social History of Timbuktu

name: Songhai Imperial Army
description: A professional army included cavalry, infantry, and a fleet of war canoes on the Niger River. Slave soldiers and cavalry formed the core of Songhai military power.
key_roles: Askia|Hi Koi (Navy Commander)|Balama (General)|Cavalry Commander|Slave Soldier|Canoe Warrior
sources: Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire

name: Ashanti Confederacy
description: A confederation of chiefdoms united under the Asantehene who sat on the Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi), symbol of national unity. Provincial chiefs retained local authority.
sources: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century

name: Ashanti Social Ranks
description: Status derived from matrilineal clan membership, office holding, and wealth. Royal clans provided rulers, while other clans held hereditary positions in the bureaucracy.
sources: McCaskie, State and Society in Pre-Colonial Asante

name: Ashanti Shrine Priests and Abosom
description: A complex religious system with the supreme god Nyame, lesser deities (abosom), and ancestors (nsamanfo). Shrine priests (akomfo) served as intermediaries and healers.
sources: McCaskie, State and Society in Pre-Colonial Asante

name: Ashanti Matrilineal Abusua
description: The abusua (matrilineal clan) determined inheritance, succession, and identity. A person belonged to their mother's clan, though the father's ntoro (spiritual element) was also recognized.
sources: Fortes, Kinship and the Social Order

name: Ashanti Judicial System
description: Chiefs adjudicated disputes with council advice. The Asantehene served as supreme judge. Oath-swearing was a formal legal mechanism to bring cases to court.
sources: Rattray, Ashanti Law and Constitution

name: Ashanti Military
description: A well-organized army with divisions named after cardinal directions. Firearms acquired through trade supplemented traditional weapons, and military service was a duty of free men.
sources: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century

name: Benin Kingdom
description: The Oba (king) ruled with divine authority, supported by a complex hierarchy of palace chiefs (uzama), town chiefs (eghaevbo n'ore), and palace associations.
key_roles: Oba|Uzama (Hereditary Chief)|Eghaevbo N'Ore (Town Chief)|Eghaevbo N'Ogbe (Palace Chief)|Iyase (War Chief)
sources: Bradbury, Benin Studies

name: Benin Social Organization
description: Society was organized around the palace, with title holders, guild members, and commoners in a hierarchical relationship. The brass-casting guild held particularly high status.
sources: Ben-Amos, The Art of Benin

name: Benin Craft Guilds (Igun)
description: Hereditary craft guilds produced bronze castings, ivory carvings, and other regalia for the Oba. The Igun Eronmwon (brass-casters guild) was the most prestigious.
sources: Dark, An Introduction to Benin Art and Technology

name: Benin Sacred Kingship
description: The Oba was semi-divine, performing rituals to maintain cosmic order. Ancestor altars in the palace received offerings, and the Oba mediated between the living and the spirit world.
sources: Bradbury, Benin Studies

name: Benin Imperial Army
description: The Oba commanded a powerful army that expanded the kingdom through conquest. Warriors earned titles and prestige through military service, and war chiefs held important political roles.
sources: Igbafe, Benin Under British Administration

name: Swahili City-State Governance
description: Independent city-states along the East African coast were governed by merchant-sultans or councils of elders. Each city (Kilwa, Mombasa, Zanzibar, etc.) was politically autonomous.
sources: Horton & Middleton, The Swahili

name: Swahili Urban Society
description: Swahili towns had a stratified society: waungwana (patrician merchants), commoners, and slaves. Stone houses indicated high status, while poorer residents lived in wattle-and-daub structures.
sources: Middleton, The World of the Swahili

name: Swahili Islamic Practice
description: Islam arrived via Indian Ocean trade and became central to Swahili identity. Mosques were the architectural and social centers of towns, and scholars maintained ties to the wider Islamic world.
sources: Pouwels, Horn and Crescent

name: Swahili Trade Networks
description: Swahili merchants operated extensive trade networks connecting East Africa with Arabia, Persia, India, and China. Trade goods included gold, ivory, enslaved people, and luxury imports.
sources: Sheriff, Dhow Cultures of the Indian Ocean

name: Swahili Patrician Family
description: Patrician (waungwana) families traced descent patrilineally and maintained genealogies connecting them to Arabian or Persian origins. Marriage alliances cemented mercantile partnerships.
sources: Middleton, The World of the Swahili

name: Tongan Tu'i System
description: Tonga developed a unique triple chieftainship: the Tu'i Tonga (sacred paramount), Tu'i Ha'atakalaua (secular ruler), and Tu'i Kanokupolu (executive chief), distributing sacred and secular power.
key_roles: Tu'i Tonga|Tu'i Ha'atakalaua|Tu'i Kanokupolu|Ma'atu (Lesser Chief)|Matapule (Talking Chief)
sources: Bott, Tongan Society at the Time of Captain Cook's Visits

name: Tongan Social Hierarchy
description: A highly stratified Polynesian society with the hou'eiki (chiefs) at the apex, followed by matapule (ceremonial attendants), mu'a (artisans), and tu'a (commoners).
sources: Kirch, The Evolution of the Polynesian Chiefdoms

name: Tongan Sacred Kingship
description: The Tu'i Tonga was considered divine, descended from the sky god Tangaloa. The Fale o Mua (house of the Tu'i Tonga) maintained sacred rituals and the inasi (first fruits) ceremony.
sources: Gifford, Tongan Society

name: Tongan Kainga
description: The kainga (extended family) was organized around senior and junior lines. The fahu (father's sister) held special ceremonial authority over her brother's children.
key_roles: Ulumotu'a (Family Head)|Fahu (Father's Sister)|Mehekitanga (Mother's Brother)|Senior Sibling|Junior Sibling
sources: Bott, Tongan Society at the Time of Captain Cook's Visits

name: Modern Liberal Democracy
description: Representative democracies with elected legislatures, independent judiciaries, and constitutional protections for individual rights. Separation of powers prevents concentration of authority.
sources: Dahl, On Democracy

name: Modern Western Class System
description: Socioeconomic classes based primarily on wealth, education, and occupation rather than birth. Social mobility is possible but uneven, with persistent structural inequalities.
key_roles: Upper Class|Upper Middle Class|Middle Class|Working Class|Underclass
sources: Wright, Class Counts

name: Western Constitutional Law
description: Legal systems based on either common law (Anglo-American) or civil law (Continental) traditions. Constitutional courts ensure legislative compliance with fundamental rights.
sources: Merryman & Perez-Perdomo, The Civil Law Tradition

name: Western Public Education
description: Universal compulsory education through primary and secondary schools, with public universities providing higher education. Curricula combine sciences, humanities, and vocational training.
sources: Dewey, Democracy and Education

name: Western Nuclear Family
description: The nuclear family (parents and children) became the dominant form in the 20th century, though extended family ties and diverse family structures persist and are increasingly recognized.
sources: Goode, World Revolution and Family Patterns

name: Western Gender Equality Movements
description: Progressive expansion of women's rights from suffrage through workplace equality to reproductive rights, though gender gaps persist in pay, representation, and domestic labor.
key_roles: Citizen|Feminist Activist|Legislator|Equal Opportunity Officer|Labor Union Representative
sources: Offen, European Feminisms 1700-1950

name: Western Secular-Religious Pluralism
description: Separation of church and state with freedom of religion. Diverse religious organizations operate independently while secular institutions govern public life.
key_roles: Head of State (Secular)|Religious Leader|Congregation Member|Interfaith Council Member
sources: Taylor, A Secular Age

name: Modern Professional Associations
description: Professional organizations (bar associations, medical boards, trade unions) regulate standards, credential practitioners, and advocate for members' interests.
sources: Abbott, The System of Professions

name: Roman Collegia
description: Voluntary associations (collegia) of artisans, merchants, and laborers that provided mutual aid, funeral insurance, and social fellowship. Some had political influence.
sources: Verboven, The Associative Order

name: Roman Gender and Matrona
description: Roman women of the elite class (matronae) could own property and manage businesses, but were excluded from political office. Their social influence was exercised through family networks.
sources: Treggiari, Roman Marriage

name: Athenian Metic Trade Networks
description: Metics (resident foreigners) dominated trade and manufacturing in Athens. They formed informal networks, were excluded from land ownership, and required citizen sponsors (prostates).
sources: Whitehead, The Ideology of the Athenian Metic

name: Athenian Navy and Hoplites
description: Citizen hoplites served in the phalanx while the thetes rowed in the trireme fleet. The navy was Athens' greatest military asset and the basis of its maritime empire.
sources: Hanson, The Western Way of War

name: Egyptian Women's Legal Status
description: Egyptian women enjoyed relatively high legal status, able to own property, conduct business, serve as witnesses, and initiate divorce. Royal women could serve as regent or even pharaoh.
key_roles: Queen (Great Royal Wife)|God's Wife of Amun|Noblewoman|Female Scribe|Common Woman
sources: Robins, Women in Ancient Egypt

name: Egyptian Artisan Communities
description: Specialized artisan communities like Deir el-Medina housed workers who built royal tombs. They were organized into work gangs with foremen and maintained their own courts.
sources: Meskell, Private Life in New Kingdom Egypt

name: Mongol Religious Tolerance
description: The Mongols practiced shamanism but tolerated all religions. Christian, Muslim, Buddhist, and Daoist clerics were exempt from taxation and served as advisors to the khans.
key_roles: Great Khan|Chief Shaman|Nestorian Priest|Buddhist Lama|Muslim Imam|Daoist Priest
sources: Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

name: Mongol Women's Authority
description: Elite Mongol women managed estates, conducted diplomacy, and served as regents. Khatuns (queens) presided over their own ordo (camp) and controlled substantial resources.
sources: Broadbridge, Women and the Making of the Mongol Empire

name: Mongol Uighur Script Adoption
description: Chinggis Khan adopted the Uighur script for Mongol and established schools for training administrators. The Yassa required princes and nobles to be educated in laws and languages.
sources: Allsen, Culture and Conquest in Mongol Eurasia

name: Ottoman Imperial Harem
description: The imperial harem was a complex institution where the valide sultan (queen mother) held enormous power. Concubines could rise to become haseki sultan, wielding political influence.
sources: Peirce, The Imperial Harem

name: Ottoman Gender Segregation
description: Urban Ottoman society maintained strict gender segregation. Women of the elite were secluded but managed household resources and property; rural women had more public roles.
key_roles: Sultan|Valide Sultan|Harem Woman|Free Urban Woman|Rural Woman|Female Slave
sources: Tucker, Women, Family and Gender in Islamic Law

name: Achaemenid Royal Household
description: The royal household was vast, with the queen mother holding significant influence. Royal women owned estates and commanded their own workforces as documented in Persepolis tablets.
key_roles: King of Kings|Queen Mother|Royal Wife|Prince|Princess|Household Manager
sources: Brosius, Women in Ancient Persia

name: Achaemenid Noble Education
description: Persian noble boys were educated from age 5 to 20 in riding, archery, and speaking the truth, according to Herodotus. Magi provided religious instruction and court education.
sources: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander

name: Inca Imperial Law
description: The Sapa Inca was the supreme lawgiver. Laws enforced work obligations (mit'a), prohibited theft and laziness, and regulated marriage. Punishments included death, exile, and loss of privileges.
sources: D'Altroy, The Incas

name: Inca Complementary Gender
description: Inca gender ideology emphasized complementarity. Women controlled household production and certain ritual domains; acllas (chosen women) served the state in weaving and religious roles.
sources: Silverblatt, Moon, Sun, and Witches

name: Aztec Calpulli Family
description: The calpulli was a territorial/kinship unit that allocated land, organized labor, and maintained a temple. Families within the calpulli held usufruct rights to communal land.
sources: Berdan, The Aztecs of Central Mexico

name: Aztec Women's Roles
description: Women managed households, wove textiles (a sacred activity), served as healers and midwives, and could operate in the marketplace. Goddesses like Coatlicue held cosmic power.
sources: Kellogg, Weaving the Past: A History of Latin America's Indigenous Women

name: Maya Royal Justice
description: The k'uhul ajaw served as supreme judge. Maya law was administered by batab (local lords) and holpop (community leaders). Punishments included slavery, sacrifice, and restitution.
key_roles: K'uhul Ajaw|Batab (Local Lord)|Holpop (Community Leader)|Ah Kulel (Court Official)
sources: Sharer & Traxler, The Ancient Maya

name: Maya Warfare
description: Warfare was central to Maya politics, aimed at capturing elite prisoners for sacrifice and establishing tributary relationships. Noble warriors led campaigns during dry season.
sources: Webster, The Fall of the Ancient Maya

name: Maya Royal Women
description: Elite Maya women served as regents, diplomats, and ritual participants. Queens are depicted on stelae performing bloodletting rituals and wielding political authority.
sources: Martin & Grube, Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens

name: Maurya Joint Family
description: The joint family (kutumba) was the foundation of Indian society. Multiple generations lived together under the authority of the eldest male, sharing property and resources.
sources: Thapar, Early India

name: Maurya Gurukula System
description: Boys from upper castes studied under a guru (teacher) in a residential school (gurukula), learning the Vedas, philosophy, mathematics, warfare, and statecraft.
sources: Mookerji, Ancient Indian Education

name: Mughal Elite Household
description: Elite Mughal households included the zenana (women's quarters) managed by senior women. Marriage alliances between Rajput and Mughal families cemented political relationships.
sources: Lal, The Mughal Harem

name: Mughal Judicial System
description: A multi-layered system combining sharia courts, imperial edicts (farmans), and Hindu customary law (dharmashastra). The emperor was the supreme appellate authority.
sources: Alam, The Crisis of Empire in Mughal North India

name: Medieval English Schools
description: Cathedral and monastic schools provided Latin-based education. The founding of Oxford (1096) and Cambridge (1209) created centers of higher learning for clergy and later laypeople.
sources: Orme, Medieval Schools

name: Medieval English Women
description: Women's legal status was defined by coverture; married women's property belonged to husbands. Widows gained more autonomy, and noblewomen could manage estates in their husbands' absence.
sources: Ward, Women in Medieval Europe

name: French Feudal Army
description: The French king relied on feudal levies of knights and men-at-arms, supplemented by mercenary companies. The chevauchee (raiding expedition) was a common form of warfare.
sources: Contamine, War in the Middle Ages

name: French Medieval Church
description: The Gallican Church maintained some independence from Rome. Monasteries (Cluny, Citeaux) wielded great economic and spiritual power, and bishops were major feudal lords.
sources: Lynch, The Medieval Church

name: French Medieval University
description: The University of Paris (founded c. 1150) became Europe's preeminent center of theology and philosophy. The faculty of arts, theology, law, and medicine each had their own governance.
sources: Verger, Men of Learning in Europe at the End of the Middle Ages

name: Imperial Landsknecht Army
description: Mercenary infantry (Landsknechte) became the HRE's primary military force from the late 15th century. They fought in pike formations and served emperors across European battlefields.
sources: Baumann, Landsknechte

name: HRE University System
description: German universities (Heidelberg, Prague, Vienna) spread from the 14th century. They became centers of Reformation thought and trained officials for territorial administration.
sources: Ruegg, A History of the University in Europe

name: Norse Women's Rights
description: Viking-Age women could own property, request divorce, and reclaim their dowry. Widows and unmarried women had considerable legal standing compared to many medieval European women.
sources: Jochens, Women in Old Norse Society

name: Edo Samurai Organization
description: Samurai served as hereditary retainers to daimyo, organized into hierarchical ranks. Peacetime roles included administration, policing, and maintaining martial arts traditions.
sources: Vaporis, Tour of Duty

name: Edo Tokugawa Legal System
description: Laws varied by social class. The buke shohatto regulated samurai behavior, while different codes governed commoners. Magistrates (bugyo) administered justice in cities.
sources: Henderson, Village Contracts in Tokugawa Japan

name: Edo Period Buddhism and Shinto
description: The temple registration system (terauke) required all families to affiliate with a Buddhist temple. Shinto shrines maintained their own priesthoods alongside Buddhist institutions.
sources: Tamamuro, The Development of the Temple-Parishioner System

name: Meiji Abolition of Feudal Classes
description: The Meiji government abolished the four-class system, creating a new hierarchy: imperial family, kazoku (peerage), shizoku (former samurai), and heimin (commoners).
sources: Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan

name: Meiji Legal Modernization
description: Japan adopted Western-style legal codes, blending French civil law and German constitutional law. The Meiji Constitution (1889) established an imperial parliament (Diet).
sources: Steenstrup, A History of Law in Japan Until 1868

name: Joseon Neo-Confucian Orthodoxy
description: Neo-Confucianism was the state ideology, displacing Buddhism. Confucian scholars conducted ancestral rites and managed state rituals, while Buddhism was suppressed but persisted.
key_roles: King|Chief Scholar (Daejehak)|Confucian Academy Head|Ritual Master|Buddhist Monk (Marginalized)
sources: Deuchler, The Confucian Transformation of Korea

name: Joseon Military System
description: The Five Military Commands defended the capital, while provincial armies guarded borders. Military officials held lower prestige than civil officials in the yangban hierarchy.
key_roles: King|Commander of Five Commands|Provincial Commander|Military Officer|Conscript Soldier
sources: Palais, Confucian Statecraft and Korean Institutions

name: Joseon Gender Hierarchy
description: Neo-Confucian ideology strictly limited women's public roles. Women of yangban families were secluded; widows were prohibited from remarrying; women's property rights diminished over time.
sources: Kim, The Memoirs of Lady Hyegyong

name: Khmer Temple Education
description: Temples served as centers of learning where monks taught reading, writing, Pali, Sanskrit, and Buddhist scripture. This tradition continued into the modern era.
sources: Harris, Cambodian Buddhism: History and Practice

name: Khmer Royal Justice
description: The devaraja served as supreme judge and source of law. Inscriptions document land disputes, property rights, and punishments administered through provincial courts.
sources: Vickery, Society, Economics and Politics in Pre-Angkor Cambodia

name: Mali Imperial Army
description: The mansa commanded a large army including cavalry, infantry, and river flotillas. Military expansion under Sundiata and Mansa Musa created one of Africa's largest empires.
key_roles: Mansa|Ton-Tigi (Army Chief)|Cavalry Commander|Infantry Captain|Archer|River Fleet Commander
sources: Conrad, Empires of Medieval West Africa

name: Mali Kouroukan Fouga
description: The Kouroukan Fouga (Charter of Manden) is an oral constitution attributed to Sundiata. It established rights, social organization, and dispute resolution for the Mande peoples.
key_roles: Mansa|Council of Elders|Qadi|Village Chief|Griot (Oral Legal Witness)
sources: Ki-Zerbo, Oral Tradition as a Source of African History

name: Great Zimbabwe Military
description: The state maintained warriors who defended territory and protected trade routes. Military power was linked to control of cattle and gold resources.
sources: Pikirayi, The Zimbabwe Culture

name: Great Zimbabwe Trade Networks
description: Great Zimbabwe controlled the gold trade between the interior and Swahili coast ports. Specialized artisans produced sophisticated stone architecture and metalwork.
key_roles: Trade Official|Gold Smelter|Stone Mason|Ivory Carver|Cotton Weaver
sources: Pikirayi, The Zimbabwe Culture

name: Zulu Ancestor Veneration and Diviners
description: The Zulu recognized Unkulunkulu (the creator) and honored ancestor spirits (amadlozi) through ritual sacrifices. Diviners (izangoma) and herbalists (izinyanga) served as spiritual specialists.
sources: Berglund, Zulu Thought-Patterns and Symbolism

name: Zulu Customary Law
description: The inkosi adjudicated disputes with the induna council. Offenses against the king (treason, sorcery) were capital crimes; civil disputes were settled through cattle compensation.
sources: Gluckman, The Judicial Process Among the Barotse

name: Igbo Customary Arbitration
description: Disputes were resolved through the council of elders, oath-swearing before shrines, and the judgment of oracles (notably the Arochukwu Long Juju). Restorative justice was preferred.
key_roles: Council of Elders|Oracle Priest|Title Holder|Earth Priest|Disputants
sources: Isichei, A History of the Igbo People

name: Igbo Apprenticeship and Oral Education
description: Knowledge was transmitted through apprenticeship, age-grade training, and oral tradition. Specialized skills (smithing, medicine, divination) were taught within families or guilds.
sources: Uchendu, The Igbo of Southeast Nigeria

name: Haudenosaunee Oral Education
description: Education occurred through storytelling, observation, and participation in community life. The Thanksgiving Address and creation narratives transmitted cultural knowledge across generations.
sources: Fenton, The Great Law and the Longhouse

name: Hawaiian Warrior Class
description: The ali'i maintained a warrior class for inter-island conflicts and territorial expansion. Kamehameha I used Western firearms and naval tactics to unify the islands.
sources: Kirch, How Chiefs Became Kings

name: Hawaiian Kapu Law
description: The kapu system regulated all aspects of life through sacred prohibitions. Violations were punishable by death, with the pu'uhonua (place of refuge) offering sanctuary for transgressors.
key_roles: Ali'i Nui|Kahuna Nui|Ilamuku (Executor of Kapu)|Pu'uhonua Keeper
sources: Malo, Hawaiian Antiquities

name: Hawaiian Knowledge Transmission
description: Knowledge was transmitted orally through chants (mele), genealogies (mo'oku'auhau), and apprenticeship. Halau (schools) trained experts in hula, navigation, and other specialized arts.
sources: Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology

name: Maori Utu (Reciprocity) System
