description: Maori justice was based on utu (reciprocity/balance). Wrongs required redress through compensation, counter-raids, or peace-making ceremonies to restore mana and balance.
sources: Mead, Tikanga Maori: Living by Maori Values

name: Maori Whare Wananga
description: The whare wananga (houses of learning) were sacred institutions where tohunga transmitted advanced knowledge of genealogy, astronomy, agriculture, and ritual to selected students.
sources: Best, The Whare Kohanga and its Lore

name: !Kung San Knowledge Transmission
description: Knowledge was transmitted through observation, imitation, storytelling, and shared experience. Children learned tracking, gathering, and social skills by participating in daily life from an early age.
sources: Lee, The Dobe Ju/'hoansi

name: Trobriand Sorcery-Based Social Control
description: Social order was maintained through fear of sorcery, chiefly authority, and reciprocal obligations. Chiefs mediated disputes, and suspected sorcerers faced public accusation.
sources: Malinowski, Crime and Custom in Savage Society

name: Byzantine Oikos
description: The household (oikos) was the basic social unit. Women's lives centered on the household, though elite women could hold property, found monasteries, and influence politics.
sources: Herrin, Women in Purple

name: Byzantine Trade Guilds
description: The Book of the Eparch (10th century) regulated Constantinople's guilds, controlling prices, locations, and practices of silk merchants, bakers, goldsmiths, and other tradesmen.
sources: Lopez, The Book of the Eparch

name: Abbasid Elite Household
description: Elite households included the harem, managed by senior women, with slaves, eunuchs, and concubines. Marriage alliances cemented political relationships between powerful families.
sources: Ahmed, Women and Gender in Islam

name: Songhai Patrilineal Household
description: The patrilineal extended family was the basic unit. Polygyny was practiced among the elite. Both Islamic and pre-Islamic kinship norms influenced family structure.
sources: Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire

name: Ashanti Oral and Artisan Education
description: Knowledge was transmitted through oral tradition, apprenticeship in craft guilds, and initiation into abosom priesthood. Royal court officials trained in Ashanti history and law.
sources: Rattray, Ashanti

name: Benin Patrilineal Family
description: Patrilineal extended families occupied compounds with the eldest male as head. Primogeniture determined succession to the Oba and to lesser titles within each lineage.
sources: Bradbury, Benin Studies

name: Benin Royal Justice
description: The Oba served as supreme judge, delegating judicial authority to chiefs. Offenses against the Oba were treated as treason. Trial by ordeal and oath-swearing were common legal mechanisms.
sources: Igbafe, Benin Under British Administration

name: Swahili Islamic Courts
description: Qadis administered justice based on Shafi'i school of Islamic law. Cases involving trade, inheritance, and family disputes were adjudicated in the mosque or court of the sultan.
sources: Pouwels, Horn and Crescent

name: Swahili Quranic Schools
description: Education centered on Quranic schools (chuo) where children learned Arabic script, Quran recitation, and Islamic studies. Advanced students traveled to Hadramawt or Oman for further learning.
sources: Middleton, The World of the Swahili

name: Tongan Maritime Warfare
description: Tongan chiefs maintained war fleets of large double-hulled canoes (kalia). Tonga projected military power across western Polynesia, establishing tributary relationships with Samoa and Fiji.
sources: Kirch, The Evolution of the Polynesian Chiefdoms

name: Tongan Chiefly Law
description: The tu'i and lesser chiefs administered justice based on custom and chiefly authority. Tapu (taboo) violations were punished severely, and chiefly decrees had the force of law.
sources: Gifford, Tongan Society

name: Tongan Oral Knowledge Systems
description: Knowledge of navigation, genealogy, history, and ritual was transmitted orally by specialists. Master navigators taught star paths, ocean currents, and wayfinding techniques.
sources: Bott, Tongan Society at the Time of Captain Cook's Visits

name: Modern Western Professional Armed Forces
description: Professional volunteer armed forces organized into army, navy, and air force branches. Civilian control of the military through elected officials is a fundamental democratic principle.
sources: Huntington, The Soldier and the State

name: Maurya-Era Women's Roles
description: The Arthashastra documented diverse roles for women including spies, courtesans, artisans, and guards. However, Dharmashastra texts increasingly restricted women's autonomy.
sources: Thapar, Early India

name: Mughal Elite Women
description: Mughal elite women wielded power behind the purdah. Nur Jahan effectively ruled during Jahangir's reign; Jahanara and Roshanara influenced succession politics.
sources: Lal, The Mughal Harem

name: Song Neo-Confucian Family
description: Zhu Xi codified family rituals including weddings, funerals, and ancestor worship. The extended patrilineal family remained ideal, with lineage trusts (yizhuang) supporting clan members.
sources: Ebrey, Confucianism and Family Rituals in Imperial China

name: Song Dynasty Women
description: Women's status declined as Neo-Confucian ideology spread. Foot-binding began among elites, widow remarriage was discouraged, and women's property rights were curtailed compared to Tang Dynasty.
sources: Ebrey, The Inner Quarters
